tier_reason: README shows first-party output of the repo's own test_fun.cpp against libm sinf/cosf/logf/expf (213.3 vs 6238.5 M/s etc.); the Makefile gives g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -march=native, but no compiler version or CPU model ('on my computer'), so it falls short of A.

corrections.workload: test_fun.cpp: each function is evaluated over a 1024-element array of floats drawn uniformly from [0, 1) (vals_test), repeated 100,000 times for libm and 1,000,000 times for the approximations, single thread, timed with clock() and reported in million evaluations per second. The intervals [-pi, pi], [1e-10, 10] and [-10, 10] are used only for the separate error statistics (bias, mean/RMS/min/max error against libm), not for the throughput loop.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile: g++ test_fun.cpp -o test_fun -Wall -W -O3 -std=c++11 -march=native (auto-vectorisation); gcc version not stated; README says clang also works
corrections.caveats: Output is 'on my computer' with no CPU or compiler version. The README output dates from 2015 (README last changed 2015-10-22), before commit 5c3caea (2019-01-11, 'Prevents dead code optimizations in test_fun.cpp') added an asm barrier to the benchmark loop; the 2015 figures (about 1.5-2 evaluations per cycle) are too low to reflect an elided loop, but they were not re-measured on the fixed harness. The speedup is a vectorised approximation against scalar, correctly rounded libm (gcc does not vectorise sinf/logf calls without -ffast-math and libmvec), so it trades precision for speed: sinapprox max abs error 5.9e-6, cosapprox 4.0e-5, logapprox 9.1e-6, expapprox max relative error 8.6e-6; glibc libmvec or other vector math libraries (SLEEF, SVML) were not compared. Throughput inputs are all in [0, 1), which hits libm's easy small-argument paths. Not intrinsics-based despite the category: plain C written so the compiler auto-vectorises it (closer to wave 1's math-simd-linear-algebra). The mipac fork claim was not checked.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; ratios 29x/33x/36x/21x are derived from page data. Shortcomings: unspecified CPU and compiler version, accuracy-for-speed trade against scalar libm with no vector-libm baseline, README numbers predate the 2019 dead-code fix of the harness, throughput inputs only in [0, 1), not an intrinsics library. Metadata checked: MIT, 106 stars, last commit 2020-04-19 (abandoned), not a fork.

tier_reason: README reproduces the author's own run of SIMD_TriangleAABB/SIMD_TriangleAABB/SIMD_TriangleAABB.cpp against Akenine-Moeller's scalar tribox code (both versions); the VS2008 project gives Release flags but the README names no CPU or compiler version, so first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: SIMD_TriangleAABB.vcproj (Visual Studio 2008 format, Version 9.00) Release config: /O2 /Ob2 /Oi /Ot /Oy /GT /GL /arch:SSE2 /fp:fast, Win32 (the timer is MSVC inline __asm cpuid+rdtsc, so 32-bit x86 only); the README does not say which configuration or compiler version produced the numbers
corrections.caveats: Numbers are a copy of the author's blog post (codercorner.com/blog/?p=1118, not reachable here, post date unchecked) with no CPU stated. The harness takes one rdtsc reading (cycles/1024) per scenario over 16384 triangles, with no repetition or warm-up, and runs all four default-code scenarios before the optimized ones. The 20x best case comes from an extra early exit (vertex v0 inside the box, a point-in-AABB test) that the scalar baseline lacks and that scalar code could equally add; it is not SIMD throughput. Typical gains are 2x to 3x (author says so); hit counts match between versions (16384/16384, 16384/16384, 0/0, 12420/12420). Baseline is the author's 'more or less verbatim, not quite' copy of Akenine-Moeller's old and new tribox code, and the 'new, faster' version was slower on his machine. The harness needs MSVC (inline asm, _control87_2); the SSE kernel in TriBox_Optimized.cpp uses portable SSE intrinsics. No licence file (author asks for a tip jar), so code is reference only.

notes: All README times and speedups match the record. Shortcomings: no CPU or compiler version, single-shot rdtsc timing, best-case 20x is an algorithmic early exit absent from the baseline rather than SIMD, no licence (reference only), 32-bit MSVC-only harness. Metadata checked: 14 stars, 6 commits all on 2021-09-08 (abandoned), no licence shown, not a fork. Could also sit in wave 8 geometry-spatial.

tier_reason: Course-project report (CMU 15-618, not peer reviewed) with benchmark code in test/avx512/simd_sort_test.cpp, flags (-O3 -flto; CMakeLists adds -march=native -fopenmp) and CPU (Xeon Silver 4114), but no compiler name or version, so first-party C, one step short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Project report Table 4 (1M elements, 32-bit int, single core): avx512::sort 0.010364 s vs std::sort 0.080234 s; Table 2 states the speedup as 7.741558x. Same table: ips4o 0.035442 s, pdqsort 0.036089 s, avx256::sort 0.019070 s. Report: 'best-cast speedup of 8x on single-core and 17x on multicore AVX512' (multicore numbers shown only in a figure). Table 7 (1024 elements, 32-bit int): avx512::sort 5.689899x std::sort.
corrections.workload: gtest cases in test/avx512/simd_sort_test.cpp sort uniform random values from [-10000, 10000] (LO/HI in test/include/test_util.h, so 1M inputs hold heavy duplicates); each algorithm is timed once per case with currentSeconds() on a copy of the same input; the checked-in NNUM is 65536, so the report's 1M (2^20), 1024 and 10M runs required editing it; N must be a power of 2. Settings: 32/64-bit int and float keys and key-value pairs, single core via OMP_NUM_THREADS=1.
corrections.caveats: Course-project report, not peer reviewed; README speedup chart is an image. Compiler name and version missing (CMakeLists: -g -O3 -flto -Wall -march=native -fopenmp), and the std library tested is not named. Single-shot timings with no repetition. The report's tables contain copy errors: Table 1 (1M IPC) and Table 6 (1024 IPC) are identical, Table 4 gives avx256 and avx512 the same 64-bit int time (0.028105 s) while Table 2 gives them 1.48x and 2.93x, and Table 3's 1M 32-bit key-value times (avx512 0.0337 s slower than avx256 0.0201 s) contradict Table 4 (0.0337 vs 0.0681). Gains are uneven: at 1M the 64-bit key-value int sort (0.106933 s) and 64-bit key-value float sort (0.107151 s) are slower than std::sort (0.085000 s, 0.099286 s), and ips4o (sequential) beats avx512::sort on 3 of 8 settings at 1M (64-bit key-value int 0.044091 s, 32-bit key-value float 0.042667 s, 64-bit key-value float 0.049526 s); in the 10M AVX2 table avx256::sort is only 1.5x std::sort while ips4o is 7.4x. The 17x multicore claim has no table. Harness frees posix_memalign buffers (aligned_init in src/common.cpp) with delete, which is undefined behaviour, and seeds inputs from std::random_device, so runs are not repeatable. Fits wave 1's sorting category better than simd-intrinsics-libraries.

notes: Every number in the record appears in the report PDF. Shortcomings: course project with no compiler version, single-shot timings on a 20001-value domain, table copy errors, slower than std::sort for 64-bit key-value pairs and behind ips4o on 3 of 8 settings at 1M, multicore 17x unsupported by tables, abandoned since 2019. Metadata checked: MIT, 31 stars, last commit 2019-01-11, not a fork.
